prompt: Write a novel about a teenage heroine who grows up and ends up changing the world

outline.name: The Last Lake
outline.description: Introduce sixteen-year-old Nia Vale, her family, and Saint Orra, a city organized around a shrinking, polluted reservoir. Nia secretly maps illegal neighborhood pipes to help families in Cinder Row obtain water beyond their official credits. Her mother Amara repairs Meridian filtration towers, while Nia's younger brother Tavi struggles with a respiratory illness requiring clean water. Nia's friendship with courier Jo Saye reveals their contrasting beliefs: Nia trusts data and systems, while Jo insists that collective action matters more than evidence alone. The chapter establishes Meridian's algorithmic rule, the city's class divisions, and Nia's determination to expose what she believes is a correctable technical failure.

outline.name: The Hidden Schedule
outline.description: Nia notices that wealthy districts receive uninterrupted water even during emergency cutoffs imposed on poorer neighborhoods. She compares household schedules, reservoir levels, and maintenance records, discovering patterns that contradict Meridian's public explanations. With Jo's reluctant assistance, she uses her mechanical skill to repair and access a damaged maintenance drone, naming it Morrow. The drone retrieves fragments of internal routing data suggesting that water is being diverted outside the city. Nia becomes convinced that the Allocation Engine is concealing deliberate political choices. Amara warns her not to mistake suspicion for proof, but Nia decides that obtaining the complete records is worth the risk.

outline.name: Morrow's Memory
outline.description: Nia and Jo investigate abandoned pumping infrastructure while Morrow reconstructs corrupted files. They uncover evidence of a concealed pipeline carrying reservoir water toward wealthy coastal enclaves and private desalination reserves. More alarming sensor data indicates toxic runoff entering the northern watershed from Helix Meridian's lithium and rare-earth mines. Nia learns that Helix has a contract with Meridian to build a privatized desalination complex once the reservoir is declared irrecoverable. She sees the shape of a manufactured crisis but struggles to explain the evidence without exposing her mother and neighbors. Jo urges her to build allies before releasing anything; Nia instead prepares a broadcast under her own control.

outline.name: The Broadcast Wall
outline.description: Nia and Jo project maps, routing records, and sensor readings across the walls of Cinder Row. The revelations spark neighborhood meetings, anger, and the first public protests against Meridian. Some residents are inspired, while others fear that Nia's accusations will bring retaliation. Meridian responds with a polished countercampaign claiming the maps are fabricated and that unauthorized pipes caused the shortages. Nia's certainty hardens into defiance when technicians quietly confirm that some of her data is genuine. During a raid on her home and Amara's workplace, Amara refuses to certify falsified filtration reports. She is arrested for sabotage, Tavi's medical allocation is revoked, and Nia flees with Morrow and the surviving records.

outline.name: Under the Reservoir
outline.description: Nia and Jo escape Saint Orra through disused irrigation tunnels beneath the reservoir basin. The journey exposes the physical consequences of Meridian's policies: abandoned districts, contaminated pools, and families moving through the dark with stolen containers. Nia wants to return for Tavi and Amara, but Jo persuades her that the records must survive. They emerge into the dry agricultural belt and are taken in by Farid Anwar, a farmer whose land has been damaged by mining runoff. Farid introduces them to the Open Current, a loose network of organizers, engineers, displaced families, and young couriers. Nia expects the network to help her reveal the truth, but immediately clashes with its distrust of centralized leadership.

outline.name: Open Current
outline.description: Nia meets the Open Current's principal members: refugee radio operator Lio Chen, hydrologist Dr. Sera Okafor, and former municipal engineer Tomas Vale, Nia's estranged uncle. The group debates whether to prioritize public exposure, direct sabotage, emergency water delivery, or watershed restoration. Rural members resent city activists who treat farms as symbols, while refugees fear that both sides will abandon them when supplies diminish. Nia withholds some of the stolen records and proposes a single coordinated operation based on her calculations. Her brilliance impresses several younger members, but Jo recognizes that Nia is already trying to make the network dependent on her.

outline.name: The Wrong Calculation
outline.description: Nia takes control of an emergency water shipment and secretly redirects it according to her model of maximum social benefit. The decision sends water away from Farid's settlement toward a larger population center, leaving a seed bank unprotected during a heat wave. Crops fail, and years of agricultural work are lost. Farid confronts Nia publicly, arguing that she treated people as variables rather than partners. The Open Current fractures, with some members demanding that Nia be expelled and others defending her intentions. Nia discovers that key records needed to prove the Helix conspiracy were destroyed, meaning her evidence can be dismissed as incomplete. For the first time, she realizes that being right may not be enough.

outline.name: Many Witnesses
outline.description: Sera challenges Nia to rebuild the case through independently verifiable evidence rather than a single stolen archive. The Open Current establishes community-owned sensor stations in farms, refugee camps, and city neighborhoods. Residents learn to inspect the data, dispute readings, and add testimony about contamination and water diversions. Nia initially resists surrendering control of the network, fearing sabotage and misinformation, but Jo forces her to confront the resemblance between her methods and Meridian's closed system. Farid agrees to help if the project supports watershed recovery rather than only political exposure. Nia begins repairing relationships by listening to people whose needs contradict her preferred plan.

outline.name: The Living Map
outline.description: The Open Current turns from evidence gathering to practical survival. Engineers repair old canals, communities restore wetlands, and local assemblies decide how to divide scarce water among farms, refugees, and urban neighborhoods. Nia designs an open mapping platform that makes every allocation visible and revisable. Her work is now collaborative rather than secretive, and she learns to accept corrections from people with less technical training but deeper local knowledge. Morrow becomes a symbol of shared stewardship instead of Nia's private tool. Meanwhile, intercepted messages reveal that Helix agents are planning to destroy the wetland sites and blame the attack on the Open Current.

outline.name: The Price of Proof
outline.description: Meridian escalates repression by cutting power to rebellious districts, arresting organizers, and broadcasting claims that the Open Current is a terrorist movement. Helix agents sabotage restoration sites, and Farid is killed after refusing to sell his land. His death devastates Nia and exposes the cost of treating truth as a shield against violence. Amara is transferred to a remote detention facility, while Tavi's health worsens. Some members demand a centralized emergency command under Nia, believing only speed can save them. Nia is tempted to accept, but Jo and Sera remind her that a movement built around one gifted leader would reproduce the old system and collapse if that leader were captured.

outline.name: The Mesh
outline.description: Lio helps Nia transform Morrow's damaged transmitter into a mesh-broadcast system linking thousands of small independent stations. The network distributes sensor readings, repair instructions, witness testimony, and local decisions without relying on Meridian's communication grid. Nia broadcasts a carefully documented account of the diversions and contamination, but the broadcast becomes powerful only when ordinary people compare their own data and confirm the pattern. Meridian technicians leak the Allocation Engine's source code, revealing that political priorities were hidden inside supposedly neutral calculations. Workers in the coastal enclaves disclose the private pipelines, and families in Saint Orra begin opening illegal connections to displaced communities. Nia understands that her role is not to speak for everyone, but to help everyone speak to one another.

outline.name: The Dry Siege
outline.description: The revelations trigger mass strikes, coordinated occupations of pumping stations, and a wave of civil disobedience across Saint Orra and the agricultural belt. Meridian attempts a final crackdown by shutting down the main filtration towers, gambling that thirst will restore obedience. Nia and the Open Current must coordinate a response without becoming a command hierarchy. Inside detention, Amara works with imprisoned technicians to interrupt the shutdown sequence. Tavi, despite his fragile health, helps organize emergency clinics and supply routes, showing Nia that care work is part of political resistance. Morrow's network begins failing under the strain, forcing Nia to trust local operators and relinquish direct control.

outline.name: The Towers Hold
outline.description: As filtration systems fail and violence threatens to spread, Amara sabotages Meridian's shutdown from inside, keeping the towers operating long enough for Open Current engineers to seize them. Nia coordinates public assemblies rather than issuing unilateral orders, allowing neighborhoods to choose priorities and report their needs. Meridian security forces lose cohesion when technicians, patrol officers, and municipal workers refuse to enforce impossible directives. Helix executives attempt to flee with financial records and water contracts, but leaked evidence exposes their role. The Authority collapses, though the victory is chaotic: reservoirs remain poisoned, essential districts are unsafe, and no one possesses a complete plan for what comes next.

outline.name: After the Fall
outline.description: In the aftermath, Nia becomes an international symbol of the uprising while Saint Orra confronts the limits of victory. Helix officials flee or reinvent themselves as reformers, trials begin, and rival factions argue over whether the old infrastructure should be nationalized or dismantled. The reservoir cannot be restored, so whole neighborhoods must be abandoned through a painful managed retreat. Nia's family loses its home in Cinder Row; Amara survives but cannot return to tower work, and Tavi remains ill. Nia helps establish elected Water Councils, transparent data trusts, community treatment plants, and legal protections defining water as a shared public right. She refuses a formal executive role, though many supporters accuse her of abandoning the movement.

outline.name: The Commons Assembly
outline.description: Years later, an adult Nia oversees the first global Water Commons Assembly. Nations facing their own water crises propose replacing Meridian's monopoly with a powerful centralized authority, arguing that only unified control can prevent future collapse. Nia recognizes the old logic beneath the new language and remembers her younger self's belief that justice depended on possessing the complete answer. She advocates a distributed system of local councils, public scientists, farmers, workers, and displaced communities, with open records and mechanisms for constant revision. The resolution is imperfect and fiercely contested, but it establishes a living global commons rather than a new monopoly. Watching young delegates take responsibility for decisions she once would have claimed alone, Nia understands that changing the world means creating structures through which people can continue repairing it together.

chapters.name: The Last Lake
chapters.content:
## The Last Lake

By dawn, Saint Orra had begun to ration the sky.

The filtration towers along the reservoir clicked awake, drawing the first gray light through their lattices of pipes. Beyond them, the lake lay in its concrete basin, green-brown and shrinking. Warning stones stood exposed along the shore, their numbers crusted with salt. The air smelled of algae and hot metal.

A loudspeaker crackled.

“Civic water credits for District Seven remain unchanged. Conservation protects every resident.”

Nia Vale tightened the strap of her satchel and crouched beside a storm drain. Cinder Row was still dark. At this hour, the city belonged to pipes.

She lifted the drain cover with her screwdriver. Warm air rose from below. Her flashlight found the narrow blue line she had marked two nights earlier. It ran east beneath the road, crossed a service channel, and vanished beneath a wall bearing the silver Meridian seal.

Nia drew the route in her notebook.

The official map showed no line there. The official map showed equal pressure, equal access, equal need. Nia had learned to trust what the city forgot to erase.

At the pipe’s joint, someone had fitted a hand-made valve from rubber and wire. A thread of water trembled from it. She placed a collection cup beneath the leak. The first drops were brown. Then they cleared.

“Nia!”

She nearly knocked over the cup. Jo Saye stood at the mouth of the alley, her orange courier jacket bright against the dark. Her bicycle leaned beside her.

“You’re going to get arrested,” Jo said.

“I’m collecting three liters.”

“That’s how it starts. Three liters, then a prison uniform, then I explain to your mother why I helped bury you under a filtration tower.”

“You’re early.”

“I’m always early. It’s one of my few marketable qualities.”

Jo tossed her a square of filter cloth. Nia caught it and capped the cup.

“Did you bring the connector?”

Jo folded her arms. “Did you bring the part where you explain that stealing water isn’t stealing?”

“It’s already leaking.”

“Into the street.”

“Because Meridian set the pressure too high.”

“So you’re repairing their mistake by stealing their leak.”

“Redirecting it.”

“Crime with better grammar.”

Nia ignored her and checked the pipe’s vibration. Water moved through it steadily, enough to supply several buildings if the pressure held. Yet the homes along Cinder Row had received only four hours of flow the previous day, and half of that had been brown.

She opened her notebook to pages crowded with columns: building numbers, credit balances, flow times, pressure readings, illness reports copied from the clinic board. The Allocation Engine was supposed to measure population, risk, and available supply, then calculate the fairest route.

But fair routes did not explain why Cinder Row went dry before its credits were exhausted. They did not explain why the terraces across the reservoir kept their gardens green.

“Tonight,” Nia said, “we connect this to the row houses.”

Jo glanced toward the lake. “Tonight, you sleep.”

“Tavi needs humidified water.”

“He needs a doctor.”

“He needs both.”

Jo’s expression softened. “How bad?”

Nia closed the notebook. “He woke coughing again.”

Their apartment stood three floors above a shuttered laundromat. Amara kept it spotless despite the cracked walls and unreliable water. She said cleanliness was a form of defiance.

When Nia returned, her mother was fastening the copper tabs of her Meridian repair coat. A smear of black sealant marked one cheek.

“You were out before the first bell,” Amara said.

“I couldn’t sleep.”

“That isn’t permission.”

Nia placed the cup on the counter. “I found a pressure fault near Seventh.”

“You found a reason to be arrested near Seventh.”

“Why does everyone keep saying that?”

“Because you keep giving us reasons.”

From the adjoining room came a wet, rattling cough.

Tavi lay curled beneath two blankets, though the apartment was warm. He was ten, narrow as a reed, with a ceramic breathing mask over his mouth and nose. The machine beside him clicked unevenly.

“Morning,” he whispered.

“Morning.”

“Did the lake get smaller?”

“It always gets smaller.”

“Then you should measure it.”

“I did.”

He smiled faintly. “You measure everything.”

“It’s useful.”

Amara appeared in the doorway. “His clean-water allocation was reduced again.”

Nia turned. “Why?”

“Risk recalculation.”

“That makes no sense. His condition is documented.”

“The Engine says household demand exceeded projected need.”

“He’s sick.”

“The Engine knows he’s sick.”

“Then it’s wrong.”

Amara’s gaze settled on her daughter. “Systems can be wrong. People can be wrong. The difference is that systems don’t like being told.”

“I can prove it.”

“Proof is not protection.”

“Without proof, they keep doing this.”

Amara looked toward the window. A Meridian truck rolled past, its tanks sealed and numbered. Two children followed it with empty containers until a guard waved them away.

“Go to school,” she said. “Then come home.”

Nia wanted to argue, but Tavi began coughing. She adjusted his mask and held his shoulder until the spasm passed.

By noon, Saint Orra had divided itself into colors.

Cinder Row’s pipes were painted red, though dust covered most of the paint. The central districts were silver, with public taps and inspection kiosks. Beyond the reservoir, the wealthy terraces shone blue-white beneath sun shields. Their gardens drank through private irrigation lines, according to rumor, and their fountains ran at night while the rest of the city slept.

At school, a wall-sized display showed the reservoir as a blue circle.

STABLE, it read.

Nia stared at the shrinking ring around it. The lake had fallen below the lowest warning mark three months earlier. Someone had simply moved the mark.

In civic mathematics, their teacher praised the Allocation Engine.

“It removes bias,” he said. “No official can favor a district, family, or political interest. The numbers decide.”

Nia raised her hand. “What if the numbers are incomplete?”

“Then the system requests better data.”

“What if someone chooses which data goes in?”

“Nia.”

“What if the system is designed to call some people low priority?”

A boy from the blue district laughed. Behind the teacher, the display pulsed:

FAIRNESS IS MEASURABLE.

After school, Jo waited beside the bike racks with two parcels strapped to her back.

“You look murderous,” she said.

“The reservoir reading is false.”

“You say that like it’s new.”

“The warning thresholds were changed.”

“Did you ask the lake?”

“I checked maintenance records.”

“Of course you did.”

Nia wheeled her bicycle into the street. “I’m going to map every unauthorized connection in Cinder Row.”

“Every one?”

“Then I’ll compare the routes to household credits.”

“And after that?”

“I’ll show Meridian.”

Jo stopped. “You think Meridian has a door marked Show Meridian?”

“I’ll find one.”

“That’s your problem. You believe every locked door is waiting for the correct key.”

Nia looked toward the towers rising above Saint Orra, silver ribs against the sky.

“If the distribution model is wrong,” she said, “we can fix it.”

“What if it isn’t wrong?”

“Then what?”

“What if it’s doing exactly what someone wants?”

A siren sounded near the reservoir. Somewhere, a gate clanged shut.

Nia thought of Tavi’s reduced allotment, the brown water in her cup, and the blue terraces drinking through the night.

“Then I’ll find out,” she said.

Jo handed her one of the parcels. “Your mother’s lunch. She left it at the depot.”

“You could have delivered it.”

“I am delivering it. To you.”

“That isn’t how courier work functions.”

“Collective efficiency,” Jo said. “Try it sometime.”

They rode into Cinder Row as the afternoon flow began. Residents emerged carrying jugs and cracked buckets. At the first public tap, the queue stretched around the block while a Meridian meter blinked red above it.

Nia slowed beside a wall and opened her notebook.

Jo groaned. “Nia.”

But Nia was already drawing the streets, drains, and pressure valves—every place where water moved unseen beneath Saint Orra.

The lake was dying. The city insisted it was stable.

Nia intended to measure the difference.

chapters.name: The Hidden Schedule
chapters.content:
## The Hidden Schedule

By seven in the morning, Cinder Row had been cut off twice.

The first cutoff came with a shudder in the pipes and a cough from every tap. The second arrived without warning. One moment water ran brown into collection buckets; the next, the pipes knocked hollow and went silent.

“Emergency conservation event,” announced the wall panel. “Duration: twelve minutes. Thank you for protecting Saint Orra’s future.”

Tavi sat at the kitchen table with his breathing mask pressed over his nose and mouth. The machine beside him clicked damp air through its tube. Its reservoir was nearly empty.

“Let the future wait,” Amara said.

She crossed the room in her gray Meridian repair jacket and took the glass from Nia’s hand. The water inside was cloudy.

“Don’t use that for Tavi.”

“It’s clearer than yesterday.”

“That isn’t the same as clean.”

The panel changed.

**CINDER ROW: TEMPORARY REDUCTION, 06:58–07:10.  
CAUSE: RESERVOIR PRESSURE INSTABILITY.  
DISTRIBUTION PRIORITY: MEDICAL, INFRASTRUCTURE, AND HIGH-RISK ZONES.**

“Tavi is medical,” Nia said.

“His credits were recalculated.”

“Because he had three good hours?”

“He had a better week.”

“He had three good hours.”

Amara did not answer. She checked the breathing machine, then the nearly empty water reservoir.

At seven twelve, the faucet began to run again.

Nia went to the window. Saint Orra climbed from the reservoir’s old floodplain toward the wealthy terraces, all pale stone and blue glass. Behind their walls, trees stood green in the drought.

A fountain glittered in the morning sun.

Then another.

Nia took out her slate. During the night, she had copied the public schedules for seven districts and added pressure readings gathered from the unauthorized pipes beneath Cinder Row.

Reservoir pressure: falling.  
Cinder Row flow: interrupted.  
North Market flow: reduced.  
Terraces Nine through Fourteen: uninterrupted.

The public display at the tram station had reported an emergency cutoff across the city at six fifty-eight. The fountains had continued.

“Stop staring at them,” Amara said.

“I’m measuring.”

“With your eyes?”

Nia turned the slate toward her. “The schedules don’t match the pressure reports.”

Amara glanced at the figures. “Reports can be wrong.”

“Seven districts can’t be wrong in the same direction.”

“No. But the person reading them can be.”

She handed back the slate. “Observations are not proof.”

Nia hated that answer because it was careful, and because careful answers had kept Meridian alive for generations.

At school, she compared the schedules beneath her desk while Instructor Pell explained the Allocation Engine.

“The Engine continuously balances projected need against available supply,” he said. “This prevents panic and eliminates favoritism.”

Nia raised her hand.

Pell sighed before calling on her. “Yes, Vale?”

“What inputs does it use for projected need?”

“Population, medical risk, infrastructure requirements, weather models, and household credits.”

“Who chooses the weights?”

“The weights are publicly audited.”

“Which audit?”

A few students laughed. Pell folded his hands.

“The Engine is designed to remove personal bias.”

“If the data is incomplete, does it remove that bias too?”

“The system accounts for uncertainty.”

“What if the uncertainty is entered deliberately?”

The room quieted.

Pell’s mouth tightened. “Then that would be a criminal act, not a flaw in the model.”

“So it can happen.”

“Anything can happen. That does not make speculation useful.”

Nia looked at her schedule grid and wrote in the margin: **criminal act acknowledged as possible.**

Jo waited outside the gates, leaning against his courier bicycle. His orange jacket was damp from a recent wash, and he wore the expression of someone who had already decided she was unreasonable.

“You missed lunch,” he said.

“I was working.”

“You were glaring at numbers.”

She showed him the grid as they walked.

Cinder Row: four interruptions in two days.  
South Blocks: three.  
East Exchange: two.  
Terraces Nine through Fourteen: none.

Jo studied it. “Maybe the terraces have separate reservoirs.”

“Then Meridian should list them.”

“Maybe they’re hospitals.”

“There are fountains outside private residences.”

“Very luxurious hospitals.”

“Jo.”

“I’m testing alternatives.”

“You’re making jokes.”

“Both can be true.”

Nia tapped the slate. “The cutoff notice said all districts. The maintenance records say pressure was unstable at the southern intake. But the pressure dropped only below the old civic boundary.”

“Which means?”

“Someone is overriding the Engine.”

“Or your records are incomplete.”

She stopped. “That’s not an accusation.”

“It’s a reminder. You keep saying the system can be repaired if we find the error. What if the error is that it was never meant to work for everyone?”

Nia looked toward the terraces, where the fountains flashed between buildings.

“Then I’ll find that too.”

The damaged maintenance drone was stored behind the old pumping depot, in a cage for equipment too obsolete to repair and too valuable to discard. Jo had acquired the access token by trading two express deliveries and a favor he refused to describe.

“You owe me,” he said as the lock opened.

“I owe you several things.”

“I’m making a list.”

The drone lay beneath a tarp, the size of a toolbox. One rotor was missing, its camera lens cracked, and corrosion spread around the charging port.

“Morrow,” Jo said.

“That’s a terrible name.”

“It means tomorrow.”

“It means a day that hasn’t happened.”

“Exactly. Hopeful.”

Nia removed the casing. Inside, a power bus had been bridged with copper foil. The memory core was sealed behind a Meridian diagnostic lock.

“Can you open it?” Jo asked.

“Can you stop breathing on it?”

“I’m supervising.”

She replaced the fractured contact, cleaned the memory points, and soldered a trimmed fan blade into place of the missing rotor. When she connected the battery, the drone twitched.

One lens brightened.

“Maintenance unit M-ORROW,” it said through static. “Status—”

Jo pressed both hands over his mouth.

Nia ignored him and fed the drone an old tower-maintenance sequence Amara had once taught her. The lock resisted, then opened a narrow directory.

Most of the files were corrupted.

**TRANSFER NODE 7—  
DESTINATION: [ERROR]  
VOLUME: 18,000—  
PRIORITY: CIVIC—  
OVERRIDE: M—**

The file ended in static.

Jo’s voice lost its humor. “Could be a hospital.”

“Outside the city?”

“How do you know it’s outside?”

“Node Seven isn’t in the municipal grid.”

Nia opened another fragment. A blue route appeared, beginning at the reservoir’s western intake. It passed beneath the upper terraces, crossed the industrial belt, and vanished beyond Saint Orra’s boundary.

The destination field was blank.

She copied the files onto three drives.

That evening, Amara found her in the laundry alcove with the drone spread open across the floor.

For a moment, she only stared.

“Where did you get that?”

“Meridian storage.”

“Nia.”

“It was abandoned.”

“That doesn’t mean it was yours.”

Nia showed her the routing fragments. Amara read them twice.

“Transfer Node Seven,” she said.

“You know the designation?”

“I know the designation. Not the destination.”

“It carries eighteen thousand units beyond the city.”

“Eighteen thousand what?”

“Cubic units, probably. The record is damaged.”

“Probably.”

Nia clenched her hands. “You always do this. You make every fact smaller.”

“I’m trying to keep you from making your conclusion larger than the evidence.”

“What if proof is being deleted?”

“Then you need more than one damaged file.”

“I need the complete records.”

Amara looked toward the room where Tavi slept. “And what will you risk to get them?”

Nia thought of the fountains above the city, shining through the cutoff. She thought of the pipe beneath Cinder Row bearing Meridian’s seal, and the hidden route leaving Saint Orra while people below waited beside dry taps.

“Whatever it takes,” she said.

Her mother’s face changed—not fear exactly, but the recognition of fear arriving.

Nia closed the drone’s casing and lifted it from the floor.

Morrow, Jo had called it.

Tomorrow, Nia thought, would have to be found in the records.

chapters.name: Morrow's Memory
chapters.content:
## Morrow’s Memory

The old pumping depot stood beyond the western freight line, where Saint Orra’s buildings gave way to rusted warehouses and salt-burned lots. Meridian had fenced it years ago, after the reservoir fell below the western intake level.

Jo slipped through a gap beneath the fence and held it open.

“Municipal enough?” she asked.

“I’m not municipal.”

“You complain about civic policy constantly. That’s practically employment.”

Morrow rolled after them on three uneven wheels, its blue casing streaked with dust. The maintenance drone’s camera flickered as it scanned the yard. Beyond the abandoned pumps, the intake canal lay dry except for a ribbon of black water shining between slabs of salt.

Nia unfolded the map she had printed at school. Transfer Node 7 appeared as a blue line interrupted by squares of corrupted code. It began at the western intake, passed beneath Terraces Nine through Fourteen, crossed the industrial belt, and vanished beyond the city boundary.

The drone had not identified its destination.

“Where would you hide a pipeline?” Jo asked.

“Somewhere no one has reason to inspect.”

“Then we should look somewhere important.”

“All of Saint Orra is important to someone.”

“Exactly.”

Morrow turned toward a low service building at the yard’s edge.

Nia followed it inside. The air smelled of old metal and lake mud. Pumps stood beneath tarps, their housings furred with white mineral deposits. Most control panels had been stripped, but one remained bolted to the wall. The Meridian seal had been painted over.

Jo caught Nia’s wrist as she reached for it. “Maybe don’t touch suspicious machinery until we know whether it explodes.”

“It’s a diagnostic port.”

“Meridian has never let technical distinctions stop an explosion.”

Nia opened the panel. Dust spilled across her fingers. She connected Morrow’s adapter to the port and waved the drone closer.

For several seconds, nothing happened. Then the panel clicked. A dead screen blinked awake, filling with pale strings of code.

Morrow emitted a low, warbling tone.

“Is that good?”

“It’s reading the local maintenance cache.”

“Which means?”

“Be quiet.”

“I’m always quiet.”

Nia looked at her.

“Quiet-ish.”

Morrow sorted the fragments by date, reconstructing damaged indexes from repeated labels. Pressure reports appeared, followed by valve inspections and emergency closures.

Then three lines assembled on the screen:

**WESTERN INTAKE: INACTIVE**  
**MUNICIPAL FEED: 0**  
**TRANSFER PRESSURE: MAINTAINED**

Nia stared. “Run it again.”

The same record appeared in three separate files. The western intake was officially inactive, yet pressure was being maintained in a line leaving the reservoir.

She enlarged the diagram. The route curved beneath the upper terraces, then angled northwest along the old freight corridor toward the coast.

Jo leaned closer. “Maybe the system forgot to update itself.”

“The pressure sensors were active.”

“Maybe they forgot those too.”

Nia thought of Cinder Row’s brown water and twelve-minute allocations. She thought of the fountains above them, running through every emergency cutoff.

Morrow chirped. A document opened beneath the route diagram, marked with a Helix Meridian authorization code.

Helix owned the northern mines, the mineral-processing plants, and half the city’s construction contracts. Its advertisements promised a bright, sustainable future beneath blue reservoirs.

The authorization described a “strategic export reserve” and “coastal continuity partners.” A list of destinations followed:

**PELAGOS ENCLAVE**  
**ASTER REACH**  
**NORTHLIGHT RESERVE**

Jo read them twice. “Those are outside the municipal water compact.”

“They have desalination plants.”

“Then why are they taking reservoir water?”

Nia scrolled through the file. “For blending. Their desalination output is unstable. Reservoir water improves mineral balance.”

Jo’s expression sharpened. “They’re using our water to make their private water better?”

“It’s not about taste.”

“That is somehow worse.”

The records showed eighteen thousand units per cycle. Then twenty-two. Then thirty. The withdrawals increased as Saint Orra’s emergency cutoffs became more frequent.

At the bottom of the authorization was a projected completion date for a new facility:

**HELIX MERIDIAN COASTAL DESALINATION COMPLEX**

Beside it, a line read:

**Construction to commence upon official declaration of reservoir irrecoverability.**

Nia stared at the date. The contract had been signed two years before the reservoir received its latest emergency classification—before the contamination spike, before the warning thresholds changed, before Tavi’s allocation was reduced.

Jo’s voice was quiet. “They were waiting for the lake to be declared dead.”

A sound came from outside.

Both girls killed their lamps. Morrow folded its camera arm and rolled behind a pump housing. Through a crack in the door, Nia saw two figures in gray field coats crossing the yard.

Helix surveyors. Their boots were clean.

One raised a handheld sensor toward the dry canal. “Readings are still elevated.”

“The northern plume should reach the watershed before the next storm,” said the other.

“Will Meridian accept the source?”

“They don’t need the source. They need the classification.”

“And the public?”

“The public needs a reason.”

The surveyors moved on.

Nia’s hand closed around the map. Morrow projected another file, this one from a remote environmental station. The data was corrupted, but the surviving readings showed sharp increases in lithium salts, rare-earth solvents, and an unfamiliar compound. The samples came from runoff channels above the northern watershed.

Nia had seen those channels from the school transit: silver-gray water winding down from Helix’s open mines and disappearing beneath culverts before reaching the lake.

The pollution was being measured. Tracked. Perhaps timed.

She copied the files onto three drives, then into Morrow’s internal memory: transfer volumes, pressure reports, contract fragments, sensor readings, authorization codes.

“Enough,” Jo said.

Nia kept copying. “We have to preserve the cache.”

“We have the route.”

“We have fragments.”

“We have a contract saying they’re waiting for the lake to be declared irrecoverable.”

“We don’t have the full contract. We don’t know who signed the override. We don’t know whether the readings were altered.”

“If we stay, they may find the drone.”

Nia looked up. “This is the first real proof we’ve found.”

“It’s enough to make people listen. It isn’t enough to tell them exactly what happened.”

“People should know.”

“Yes. But if you release incomplete records, Meridian will call them fabricated, seize the rest, and blame the shortages on illegal neighborhood pipes.”

Nia thought of Amara repairing filtration towers beneath Meridian cameras. She thought of Tavi fighting for breath when the water shut off and the air grew dry.

“We can’t wait for perfect proof.”

“I didn’t say perfect. I said allies.”

“Who? Everyone is afraid.”

“Then find the people afraid of the same thing.”

Nia turned back to the screen. “I know how to present this.”

“That isn’t the same as knowing how to protect it.”

Jo crouched beside Morrow, examining its cracked casing. “It can transmit short bursts through the maintenance grid. Maybe. But it needs relays. Trusted ones.”

“I can build a transmitter.”

“You can build ten. You can’t make ten neighborhoods trust you.”

Nia looked at the drone. Its camera was scratched, its wheels mismatched, its memory full of broken things. Yet it had remembered what Meridian had tried to erase.

“What about the old civic wall?” she asked.

Jo frowned. “The projection wall?”

“It still has a public receiver. If we route Morrow through it, we can display the maps, the pressure records, the contract.”

“For how long?”

“Long enough.”

“And then?”

“Then people see it.”

“People seeing something isn’t the same as people acting.”

Nia gathered the drives. “It’s a beginning.”

Jo followed her outside. Clouds had gathered over the northern hills, dark beneath the setting sun. Rain was coming, though the forecast called it unlikely. If the runoff reached the lake, the contamination would spread through the intake channels.

Nia imagined the city panel glowing **STABLE** while poison entered the reservoir.

Jo stopped beside the fence. “Show the records to someone before you broadcast.”

Nia tucked the drives inside her jacket.

“No.”

“Nia.”

“If we show them to the wrong person, they disappear.”

“And if you show them to everyone, we disappear.”

Nia looked back at the abandoned pumps, at the hidden line carrying water beneath the city toward people who had paid to outlive it.

“I’m not asking permission from a system built to deny the problem,” she said.

Jo’s mouth tightened. “You’re not the system.”

“Not yet.”

They crossed the yard as Morrow rolled between them, its small light blinking steadily in the dark.

By midnight, Nia had chosen the wall, rebuilt the route map, and begun preparing the broadcast.

chapters.name: The Broadcast Wall
chapters.content:
## The Broadcast Wall

At midnight, the wall above Cinder Row was blank except for old rain stains and the pale rectangle where a civic announcement had been removed.

Nia stood beneath it with a coil of cable over one shoulder and Morrow tucked inside a canvas tool bag. Jo crouched beside the public receiver, swearing softly at its corroded housing.

“You said this would work,” Nia whispered.

“I said it had a receiver.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is if you’re optimistic.”

The receiver clicked. Somewhere inside the wall, a relay woke with a cough of static. Morrow’s indicator light blinked through the canvas.

Nia unfolded the first map.

It showed the western intake in blue, the municipal feeds in gray, and Transfer Node 7 as a bright line threading beneath Terraces Nine through Fourteen. She had stripped away labels that might identify the depot cache and replaced them with dates, pressure readings, and withdrawal volumes. The line ended beyond the city boundary, where she had marked the names recovered from Helix’s authorization: Pelagos Enclave. Aster Reach. Northlight Reserve.

Jo looked at the map, then at the sleeping apartments packed around the square.

“Last chance,” she said.

Nia thought of Tavi breathing through the humidifier, each breath a small mechanical struggle. She thought of the terrace fountains she had seen from the tram, spilling white water into ornamental channels while Cinder Row taps coughed air.

“No,” she said.

She pressed the transmitter.

The wall came alive.

The first image appeared crooked, then steadied: **WESTERN INTAKE: INACTIVE. MUNICIPAL FEED: 0. TRANSFER PRESSURE: MAINTAINED.**

A woman carrying two empty containers stopped in the street. A boy in a yellow coat looked up from a doorway. Within minutes, faces appeared at windows.

Nia sent the next image. The hidden route. The pressure graph. The export volumes climbing from eighteen thousand units to twenty-two, then thirty thousand per cycle.

A murmur moved through the square.

“That’s under the terraces,” someone said.

“Under ours too?”

“No. Look where it turns.”

The final map spread across the wall, reaching almost from one end to the other. At the edge of the old freight corridor, the line continued toward the coast.

Jo climbed onto a crate. “Read the destinations,” she called.

Nia did. Her voice trembled only once.

“Pelagos Enclave. Aster Reach. Northlight Reserve. These are outside Saint Orra’s water compact. The records identify our reservoir water as a strategic export reserve.”

“Strategic for who?” a man shouted.

The wall changed again. Helix Meridian’s contract fragment appeared, followed by a construction schedule for a coastal desalination complex. The signing date sat above the date of Saint Orra’s latest emergency classification by nearly two years.

Someone laughed, but there was no humor in it.

“They knew,” the woman with the containers said.

Nia displayed the environmental readings. Lithium salts. Rare-earth solvents. The unfamiliar compound from the northern runoff stations. She added photographs of silver-gray water slipping through the mine culverts.

The square erupted.

By dawn, the wall had become a meeting place.

People came from the neighboring blocks with handwritten records of their own. A laundry worker brought a notebook showing water cuts that never appeared on public schedules. A clinic attendant said three children had developed rashes after the last pressure drop. A retired pipe fitter pointed to the map and named two service tunnels Nia had missed.

“Those lines don’t go to the coast,” he said. “Not directly. They join at the old freight pump.”

Nia revised the map while he watched.

The correction made the route more complicated and more convincing.

Jo moved through the crowd, taking names and collecting copies. She made Nia explain every symbol twice, then three times, whenever people asked. At first Nia found it irritating. Each question slowed the work. Each challenge threatened to pull the evidence apart.

But when a woman named Sella asked, “How do we know these numbers weren’t planted for you to find?” Nia stopped.

“Because they agree with the pressure changes in your district,” she said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Nia looked at the woman’s lined face, at the empty container resting against her ankle.

“No,” she admitted. “It isn’t.”

By afternoon, the crowd had formed three circles around the wall. One demanded a march to the municipal offices. Another argued that the city would shut off Cinder Row entirely if they provoked Meridian. The third wanted to cut the hidden pipe immediately.

“Break the line and they lose their gardens,” a young man said.

“They’ll blame us for poisoning the lake,” someone answered.

“We’re already being blamed.”

The anger frightened Nia less than the fear. Anger moved outward. Fear folded into silence, where Meridian could use it.

Near sunset, Meridian’s response appeared on every public screen.

A woman with silver hair and a calm, sympathetic expression stood before a blue background. Behind her, the Meridian emblem rotated slowly.

“Saint Orra is experiencing a difficult but manageable environmental event,” she said. “Unauthorized neighborhood connections have disrupted pressure balance and caused uneven distribution. Images circulating through illegal projection systems are fabricated composites assembled from stolen maintenance fragments.”

The next image showed a red tangle of pipes labeled **CINDER ROW INTERFERENCE NETWORK**.

“They are asking you to believe that a secret government pipeline runs beneath the city,” the woman continued. “In truth, unlicensed diversions have deprived hospitals, schools, and compliant households. Meridian will restore fairness.”

A caption appeared beneath her:

**DO NOT TRUST UNVERIFIED DATA. REPORT UNAUTHORIZED CONNECTIONS.**

Jo watched the broadcast with her arms folded.

“They made us the villains before breakfast.”

Nia stared at the red tangle. “They don’t have the real maps.”

“They don’t need them.”

By morning, Meridian crews had painted over the projection wall. By noon, residents had scrubbed it clean and reconnected the receiver. The maps returned, now surrounded by testimony, corrections, and demands written in grease pencil.

The first protest began with forty people.

It became four hundred by the time they reached the municipal gates.

Nia walked near the front with Jo, carrying Morrow beneath her coat. People chanted for open records, for water, for the release of Amara Vale, though Amara had not yet been arrested and Nia had not told anyone about her mother’s involvement. She felt the chant strike her like a warning.

At the gate, a Meridian technician stepped from a service vehicle. He was young, perhaps twenty, with a badge turned backward on his shirt.

“You’re Nia Vale?” he asked.

She stiffened.

He glanced at the crowd, then lowered his voice. “The western intake record is real.”

Jo moved between them. “Who are you?”

“Someone who knows the pressure line was never inactive.” He swallowed. “And the environmental stations were reporting solvent traces before the official contamination date.”

“Can you prove it?” Nia asked.

His expression hardened. “That’s the problem. They erased the originals.”

He returned to the vehicle before security noticed him.

For the first time, Nia felt certainty settle inside her—not as a conclusion, but as armor. They had lied. They were still lying. Every polished denial made the truth more solid.

That evening, the raid came.

The door burst inward while Tavi was asleep.

Nia woke to boots in the corridor and the sharp crack of something breaking. Amara shouted from the kitchen. Tavi began coughing.

“Get up,” Jo hissed from the fire escape window. She had been keeping watch in the alley. “Now.”

Nia grabbed the canvas bag.

Three officers entered the room. One wore a Meridian investigation seal; the others wore municipal armor.

“Unauthorized data theft,” the officer said. “Nia Vale, step away from the equipment.”

Morrow gave a faint electronic chirp beneath the floorboard where Nia had hidden him.

She kicked the board shut.

In the kitchen, Amara stood with both hands raised. A tablet lay shattered at her feet.

“They ordered me to certify false filtration readings,” she said. Her voice was steady. “I refused.”

The officer turned toward her. “You altered a tower report.”

“I corrected it.”

“You reported safe output when the filters were failing.”

“I reported the truth.”

Tavi appeared in the doorway, barefoot and shaking. His humidifier hissed behind him.

A second officer scanned his medical band. The screen flashed amber.

“Household medical allocation revoked,” she said.

Nia’s breath vanished.

Amara lunged. “He needs that water.”

“Allocation fraud is under investigation.”

“He is ten years old.”

The officer caught Amara’s wrists and twisted them behind her. Tavi coughed so hard he bent double.

Nia wanted to attack them. The impulse rose hot and clean, simpler than thought. But Jo’s hand closed around her arm from the window.

“Now,” Jo whispered.

Amara looked at Nia.

Not at the bag. Not at the officers. At her.

“Take him,” Amara said.

Nia shook her head.

“Take the records.”

“I’m not leaving you.”

“You are not leaving me.” Amara’s eyes flicked toward Tavi. “You’re carrying us somewhere they can’t erase us.”

The officer pulled her toward the hall. Tavi reached for her, coughing.

Nia pressed herself into the darkness beside the window. Jo hauled her through. Morrow’s weight struck her ribs. Behind them, the apartment filled with shouting, the scrape of boots, and the wet, frightened sound of Tavi trying to breathe.

They crossed three roofs before the alarms began.

At the far edge of Cinder Row, Nia stopped beneath a broken vent and looked back. Their apartment window glowed with Meridian’s white searchlights. The broadcast wall flickered below, half-covered by fresh paint.

Jo caught her shoulder. “We have to move.”

Nia held Morrow against her chest. Inside his memory, the maps still existed. The pressure records. The pollution readings. The names of the coastal reserves.

Not everything had been erased.

She turned from the lights and followed Jo into the dark.

chapters.name: Under the Reservoir
chapters.content:
## Under the Reservoir

The fire escape ended three floors above the alley.

Nia climbed down anyway. Her palms slipped on cold metal, and Morrow knocked against her back inside the canvas maintenance bag. Below, Meridian floodlamps swept across Cinder Row while officers searched the apartments.

Sixteen-year-old female. Technical training. Possible access to restricted infrastructure.

Nia looked toward the Vale apartment. Their window blazed white. Tavi was still inside. His humidifier would be empty by morning. Amara had been arrested for refusing to certify false filtration readings.

“We’re going back,” Nia said.

Jo caught her wrist. “No.”

“My brother is sick.”

“I know.”

“My mother is under arrest.”

“I know that too. If we go back, they get you, Morrow, and the records. Then nobody knows Node 7 exists.”

“Tavi doesn’t need people to know.”

“He needs someone outside to get his allocation restored.”

A shadow crossed the apartment window. Nia leaned toward it, but Jo pulled her into the alley.

“Your maintenance route,” Jo whispered. “Now.”

The entrance lay behind a condemned laundry, beneath a hatch marked with an obsolete blue circle. Nia forced it open with a length of pipe. Damp, mineral air rose from below.

She hesitated.

“Tavi’s future,” Jo said quietly. “That’s what Amara told you to take.”

Nia descended. Jo followed and pulled the hatch shut. Saint Orra vanished above them.

The irrigation tunnel sloped beneath the reservoir basin. Its brick walls sweated in the dark, and old arrows pointed toward gates that had rusted open decades ago. Silt covered the floor along with ration containers, plastic bottles, and scraps of clothing.

After twenty minutes, they found a family gathered beside a shallow pool. Six people crouched around a hand pump, filling metal canisters. A girl held a rag over her mouth.

Jo raised both hands. “We’re not Meridian.”

“Everyone says that,” the woman at the pump replied.

Nia crouched beside the water. Oil shimmered across its surface. Her sensor registered solvent traces.

“Don’t drink this,” she said.

The woman laughed bitterly. “We’re boiling it.”

“Boiling won’t remove the salts.”

“Then tell Meridian.”

Nia had no answer. Jo gave the woman two purification tablets. “One per full container. Wait twenty minutes.”

The woman accepted them, eyes fixed on Morrow’s bag.

They continued.

A collapsed section forced them through a narrow gap into an abandoned district built into the basin’s old eastern rim. Houses protruded from the mud like broken teeth. A municipal marker read:

**SECTOR 12: DECOMMISSIONED FOR PUBLIC SAFETY.**

Blankets lay in doorways. A table was crusted white with minerals. Further on, another family pushed a handcart loaded with stolen containers. They passed silently through the dark.

Nia watched their shadows disappear.

“How many people live down here?” she asked.

“Whoever the schedules push out,” Jo said.

At the tunnel’s lowest point, black water covered the floor to their knees. They lifted the bag above their shoulders and waded through. Something brushed Nia’s ankle. She flinched, but Jo caught her elbow.

A ladder rose at the far wall. Above it, a circular maintenance door resisted their efforts. Nia found a pressure-release lever half submerged in grime. She wedged the pipe beneath it. Together they leaned until the mechanism shrieked and gave way.

Cold air rushed in.

They climbed through the door into a dry drainage cut beyond the reservoir’s southern wall. Dawn thinned the sky behind them. Saint Orra spread across the basin, all towers and stacked districts, appearing almost clean from a distance.

Nia turned toward it.

“We can still return.”

Jo stood beside her, soaked and shivering. “For what?”

“For Tavi.”

“And then?”

“For Amara.”

“And then?”

Nia had no answer.

They walked south into the agricultural belt.

By midday, their clothes had dried stiff with salt. Fields stretched on either side of the road, divided by cracked irrigation channels. Dead stalks rattled in the wind. A line of fruit trees stood leafless beside a ditch stained silver along its edges.

A man stepped from behind a rusted tractor with a rifle held low.

“Stop.”

Jo stopped. Nia’s hand went to the maintenance bag.

“Meridian?” the man asked.

“No,” Jo said.

“Helix?”

“No.”

“Then why are you carrying a machine like it owes you money?”

“Morrow doesn’t owe anyone money,” Nia said.

The man studied her. “That is not an answer.”

His name was Farid Anwar. He lowered the rifle and led them to a shed lined with tools and irrigation hose. He gave them lentil broth and blankets, then examined the mineral stains on their clothes.

“You came through the basin,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Then you saw what the city does not count.”

Nia set Morrow on the workbench. “Families collecting contaminated water.”

Farid’s expression tightened. “The contamination came through my land.”

She looked at him.

“Helix opened the northern pits two years ago,” he said. “They promised lined channels and sealed ponds. The first storm broke both promises. Meridian tested the runoff and called it acceptable.”

“Do you have the reports?”

“I have dead trees.”

“That isn’t proof.”

Farid laughed once. “No. It is not proof for your records.”

Jo gave Nia a warning look.

Farid poured more broth. “There are people here who know where the pipes run. People who watched their wells change color. If you want their help, don’t arrive asking them to become evidence.”

“I need to know what happened,” Nia said.

“So do we.”

The shed door opened. A young man with a radio across his chest entered, followed by a woman carrying rolled maps and a narrow-faced engineer in a dust-covered coat.

“This is Lio,” Farid said. “Sera. Tomas.”

Tomas glanced at Morrow. “That’s an old maintenance drone.”

“It still works,” Nia said.

“Barely,” Jo added.

Lio stared at her. “Is that Morrow?”

Nia stiffened. “How do you know its name?”

“Half of Cinder Row saw its eyes on the projection wall.”

Jo turned to Farid. “You said nobody knew where we were.”

“I said you needed shelter,” Farid replied. “Not anonymity.”

Sera spread maps across the workbench. “The Open Current can move you beyond the city grid. We may be able to send word toward Saint Orra, though not quickly.”

“Tavi needs medical water now,” Nia said.

“We know,” Lio answered. “Every district has someone who needs something now.”

Nia laid out her maps: the transfer route, pressure records, export volumes, contamination readings, and the Helix contract fragment.

“If we release the complete pattern, Meridian loses control,” she said.

“Do you have the complete pattern?” Sera asked.

Nia paused.

“No,” Jo said.

Sera nodded. “Then we begin with what can be verified.”

“We don’t have time for meetings while Meridian erases everything.”

“We don’t hold meetings because we enjoy them,” Farid said. “Water moves through land, and land does not obey one person’s calculation.”

Nia felt heat rise in her face. “Your land is dying because nobody calculated correctly.”

“And yours is dying because someone calculated without asking us.”

Silence settled over the shed.

Morrow’s red lamp blinked between them.

Nia looked at the gathered faces—the radio operator, the hydrologist, the farmer, the engineer. None seemed ready to surrender their decisions to her evidence.

Behind her, Saint Orra held Amara and Tavi.

Nia gathered the maps but did not put them away.

“Fine,” she said. “Show me what you know.”

Farid pulled a chair toward the table.

“No,” he said. “You show us first. Then we decide what it means together.”

chapters.name: Open Current
chapters.content:
## Open Current

Farid’s shed had once stored grain. Now it held water barrels, seed sacks, a broken tractor, and seven people pretending not to hear the wind drag dust across the walls.

Nia sat beside Morrow’s charging coil. The drone’s blue eye blinked while its damaged transmitter clicked, searching for a signal that did not exist.

A woman in a red scarf watched it. “That’s the machine from the wall.”

“I carried the signal,” she said when Nia looked at her. “Lio Chen.”

She tapped the radio pack strapped to her chest. A burn scar ran from her left ear to her collar.

“Your broadcast reached three settlements before Meridian cut the receivers,” Lio continued. “The picture broke apart, but the blue route came through clearly.”

“Morrow retrieved the records,” Nia said.

“Then it is a very polite criminal.”

“It isn’t a criminal.”

“It steals files and trespasses in restricted corridors.”

“It retrieves data.”

Jo, crouched near the door, snorted. “You’ve made a friend.”

The door opened. Sera Okafor entered with a rolled map beneath one arm. She was tall, broad-shouldered, and silver-haired, with field glasses hanging against her chest. Behind her came a man Nia recognized before she understood why.

Tomas Vale had lost weight since she last saw him. Gray threaded his hair, and he walked with a stiffness in one leg. He stopped when he saw her.

“Nia.”

“My uncle,” she said.

“Your mother’s brother,” Tomas added.

Amara had removed him from family stories years ago—not angrily, but completely.

Tomas looked at Morrow. “You rebuilt a maintenance drone.”

“I repaired it.”

“You were eight when you took apart my pressure gauge.”

“I put it back together.”

“You put it back upside down.”

“It still measured pressure.”

For half a second, his mouth almost smiled. Then he looked away. “You shouldn’t be here.”

“Neither should you.”

“No,” he said. “I shouldn’t.”

Sera spread her map across a crate. It showed the agricultural belt, the reservoir, and Saint Orra’s districts beyond it. Red marks crowded the northern watershed. Blue lines followed old canals and vanished at the city boundary.

Nia laid her own map over it. Transfer Node 7 ran from the western intake beneath the terraces, across the industrial belt, and toward the coast. She placed the pressure records beside the route.

“The freight corridor joins the transfer line here,” she said. “Pressure rises at the intake, drops at the old pump, then rises again beyond the city. The withdrawals continue even when municipal feed is listed as zero.”

Farid leaned over the map. “And this water goes to the coastal enclaves?”

“Pelagos, Aster Reach, Northlight Reserve. Their desalination systems use freshwater to stabilize mineral balance.”

“They have seawater,” said Rafi, one of the younger people by the wall.

“Not enough for continuous operation.”

“So they get ours.”

“Yes.”

“And we get what?”

Nia placed a photograph of the northern runoff on the map. Silver-gray water shone between black stones.

“Toxic contamination from the Helix mines.”

Sera touched the photograph. “These readings are not enough.”

“They match the runoff.”

“They match your conclusion. That is different.”

Nia felt heat rise in her face. “I have pressure reports, transfer volumes, authorization codes, and a Helix contract.”

“A fragment of a contract.”

“A fragment naming the coastal complex, scheduled before the contamination classification and before the emergency cutoffs.”

Sera’s expression softened. “Your brother’s suffering matters. It does not make incomplete documents complete.”

Nia thought of Tavi’s shallow breaths and the officer revoking his medical allocation. “Then we obtain the missing records. We take the freight pump, copy its cache, trace the line to the coast, and release everything together. Meridian will not be able to deny it.”

“And while you conduct your unveiling?” Farid asked.

His hands were stained with soil. Behind him, through a gap in the boards, Nia could see dead trees standing beside a silver-stained ditch.

“The wells keep changing,” he said. “Families are hauling water twelve kilometers. If you take the pump, who goes thirsty first?”

“The city has more people.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is a calculation.”

“It is a way of saying some people are acceptable losses.”

The words struck her with the force of a slap.

Lio raised his radio pack. “If we expose the route through the southern relays, other cities may pressure Meridian.”

“Other cities may send statements,” Farid said. “Statements do not fill canals.”

“Then cut the hidden pipe,” Rafi said. “Make export impossible.”

Tomas shook his head. “A rupture under pressure could flood the industrial belt with contaminated water.”

“Emergency delivery first,” said a woman beside the seed sacks. “Move stored water to the settlements.”

“Stored by whom?” Farid asked. “Every cache is guarded. Every convoy becomes a target.”

“Restore the watershed,” Sera said. “Repair diversion gates. Reopen the marsh channels. Slow the runoff before the next storm.”

“We don’t have a season,” Rafi said.

“We may not have another choice.”

The arguments tangled: exposure, sabotage, water convoys, marshes, strikes. Nia watched the lines on the maps. Every problem had variables. Population. Flow. Distance. Risk. Somewhere inside them was a correct decision.

She placed her hand over the blue route.

“I have a plan.”

The room quieted.

“We use the freight pump as the center of one operation. Lio broadcasts the transfer records through the relay stations. Tomas and I access the pump and copy its cache. Farid’s people secure the western gates so Meridian cannot divert water once the route is exposed. Sera releases the contamination readings. At the same time, emergency stores move toward the largest population centers.”

“Which centers?” Farid asked.

“Saint Orra’s southern districts first. Then the refugee camps.”

“Not here.”

Nia pointed to the city. “The numbers are larger there.”

“Here are farms feeding those numbers.”

“The farms cannot survive without water either.”

“Exactly.”

Sera studied her. “Who coordinates this operation?”

Nia hesitated only briefly. “I do.”

Jo closed her eyes.

“I know the route and pressure sequence,” Nia continued. “I know the maintenance access points. Morrow can carry the copied files and transmit from the pump. If everyone follows the schedule, Meridian cannot isolate any one group.”

Rafi leaned forward. “You can calculate patrol changes?”

“I can account for probable variations.”

Several younger members exchanged impressed looks. Suspicion shifted toward possibility. Nia felt the room begin to arrange itself around her plan.

Then Jo said, “You left something out.”

Nia turned.

Jo folded her arms. “She has more records. The authorization chain. The file marked M—. References to environmental stations.”

Sera looked at Nia. “Is that true?”

Nia touched the drive sewn into her jacket. It held a partial override code, two corrupted station reports, and a routing note naming a municipal signer whose name began with M.

“I don’t know whether they’re authentic,” she said.

“That is not why you hid them,” Jo replied.

“If they’re compromised, Meridian can use them to discredit everything.”

“Or we can test them.”

“I was preventing a false lead from destroying the case.”

“You were keeping control of the case.”

The words landed because they were true.

Tomas looked down at the map. “Your mother used to do that. Hold a repair until she understood the whole failure. Sometimes the tower collapsed first.”

Nia faced him. “You don’t get to talk about her.”

“No,” he said. “I don’t.”

Sera extended her hand. “Show us.”

Nia did not move.

Outside, metal clanged in the fields. Farid reached beneath the crate for the shotgun. Lio killed the lamp.

An engine approached along the southern road, low and steady.

In the dark, everyone waited—not for Nia’s command, but for one another’s decision.

She drew out the drive.

“Fine,” she whispered. “But we examine it together.”

Jo’s hand found hers and squeezed once.

Not forgiveness. Not yet.

A beginning, perhaps.

Nia placed the drive on the map, directly over the blue line, and listened as the engine passed beyond the fields.

chapters.name: The Wrong Calculation
chapters.content:
## The Wrong Calculation

By noon, the fields had turned white beneath the heat.

Farid’s irrigation channels were empty. Millet leaves curled inward, bean blossoms fell before fruiting, and the young trees along the western fence hung limp and gray. At the shed, three tablets lay across a packing crate while Nia studied the moving lines of the emergency distribution model.

“The convoy is twenty minutes away,” she said. “Forty-eight thousand units.”

“It is supposed to reach us,” Farid replied.

Nia enlarged the map. Red points pulsed across Saint Orra’s southern districts. Clinics there had fallen below their emergency reserves. The refugee camps along the old rail line were worse. Farid’s settlement showed amber.

“The eastern line is losing pressure,” Nia said. “If the convoy comes here, the city and camps drop below the survival threshold.”

Farid bent over the tablet. “And if it comes here, we protect the seed bank.”

“The immediate population is smaller.”

“Smaller than the city, yes.”

“The model projects more deaths if we keep the shipment here.”

Farid straightened. “Your model has never had to save a field.”

Nia ignored the remark. She had run the projection six times. The convoy could not be divided quickly enough. The first twelve thousand units had to go to the camps; the rest had to reach Saint Orra. Farid’s settlement received nothing.

Jo came into the shed, sweat darkening her collar. “The drivers are waiting for the gate signal.”

Nia turned the tablet toward her. “We need the southern diversion.”

“Farid’s route?”

“The city route is longer. If we wait for a council vote, we lose the shipment.”

Jo looked at the map, then at Nia. “You’re going to do this without telling them.”

“I’ve done the numbers.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

Outside, an engine thundered over the dirt road. Six white tankers appeared behind the fields, followed by trucks carrying filters and flexible pipe. Farid’s workers raised the western gate. The lead tanker slowed.

Nia opened the maintenance controls. The Open Current had agreed that every diversion required council approval. The council was still arguing over the freight pump and the western gates.

There was no time.

She entered Tomas’s override sequence.

**AUTHORIZED DECISION REQUIRED.**

Nia selected **EMERGENCY DISTRIBUTION**.

Jo caught her wrist. “Nia.”

“If we wait, people die.”

“Then tell them what you’re doing.”

“The convoy is here now.”

She pulled free and sent the signal.

The gate began to turn. The tanker convoy swung south, away from the settlement.

For one bright instant, relief rose in her. On the tablet, the city’s red points softened. The refugee camps climbed above threshold. Projected deaths fell.

Then Farid ran into the road, waving both arms.

The lead tanker braked, throwing dust across the ditch. A driver leaned from the cab.

“What’s happening?”

Farid pointed at Nia. “Ask her.”

Nia stepped forward. “The shipment is being redirected to Saint Orra.”

“Who authorized it?”

“I did.”

The engines idled. Behind Nia, people emerged from the sheds.

Farid came toward her. “You did.”

“We have a population emergency.”

“We have a seed reserve that feeds six settlements through winter.”

“Your reserve is not the only one.”

“No. It is the one you decided could be sacrificed.”

Nia lifted the tablet. “The distribution model shows that protecting the crops produces less immediate benefit than sending the water to the city.”

“Immediate benefit,” Farid repeated. “That is what you call people?”

“I call it a necessary comparison.”

“You call us variables.”

“The city has clinics. Children on oxygen. Buildings where people cannot leave for water.”

“And these fields become food for them.”

“Later.”

Farid’s expression hardened. “And if there is no later?”

Sera, Lio, and Tomas arrived from the neighboring shed. Others followed. The council had broken apart around them.

Nia faced the gathering crowd. “If we prioritize those at greatest risk, the shipment must go north. We can send another convoy here when the next route opens.”

Farid pointed toward the fields. “The next route opens after the heat kills the seed bank.”

“That is not certain.”

“You never asked us what could be saved.”

“I calculated what would save the most lives.”

“You calculated what happens to a field when it is denied water,” Farid said. “You did not calculate what happens to the people who depend on it, because you never asked them.”

Nia felt the crowd shift against her. “If I had asked, we would still be debating.”

“Then you should have made the argument.”

Tomas looked at the tablet. “Can you restore the original route?”

Nia glanced at the map. The city’s red points pulsed faster. She thought of Tavi’s dry humidifier and Amara’s voice in the apartment: Take his future.

“Do it,” Tomas said.

Nia reversed the diversion.

The convoy turned north. Farid watched it disappear in a cloud of dust.

By evening, the fields had begun to fail.

Workers moved between the rows with empty buckets, wetting the soil around selected plants, trying to preserve something. The northern seed bank was already lost. Three generations of drought-resistant grain had been stored there, along with bean stock and orchard cuttings. Perhaps one field could be saved if the night cooled.

Inside the equipment shed, the Open Current gathered beneath a trembling lamp.

“She should be removed from operational access,” Farid said.

“I agree,” said one of the younger couriers.

Another shook his head. “She saved the camps.”

“She stole our water.”

“Both can be true,” Sera said.

Nia stood beside the table, unable to defend herself without returning to the figures.

Tomas looked at the group. “The question is not whether Nia intended harm. It is whether anyone should make an irreversible decision alone.”

“Irreversible,” Farid said. “Does she understand that word?”

Nia looked toward the dark fields. “How much did we lose?”

Farid answered without hesitation. “The northern seed bank. Most of the beans. The orchard cuttings. Years of work.”

The word years stayed in the room.

Sera picked up the drive Nia had placed on the map the previous night. “Then we inspect the authorization files now.”

Morrow’s lens opened as Sera connected the drive. The screen filled with corrupted symbols. Nia leaned over it.

“The chain begins here,” she said. “Helix authorization, municipal override, environmental classification. If we recover the missing blocks—”

“There are no missing blocks,” Tomas said.

He pointed to the file structure. “They were overwritten.”

Sera opened the first environmental report. The station coordinates remained, but the chemical readings had been replaced with a clean-water baseline. The second file contained only its header. The contract fragment ended before the signature. The municipal signer appeared as a blank field.

Nia searched the pressure reports. Enough remained to suggest that Node 7 had carried water. Not enough established who had ordered it.

Someone had not simply damaged the evidence. Someone had selected what to destroy.

“Can any of it be restored?” she asked.

“Not from this copy,” Tomas said.

Meridian would call the records fabricated. Helix would call the pollution readings inconclusive. The missing sections would become proof that there had never been anything to find.

And Farid’s people would remember that she had taken their water.

Nia stared at the tablet. The city’s projected reserves glowed green. Beyond the shed, the fields darkened under the first wind of night.

“I was right,” she said.

No one answered.

She had been right about the hidden pipe, the exports, the poisoned watershed. She had believed that truth, once measured correctly, would force the correct action. She had believed a better calculation could protect everyone from the consequences of choosing.

But the fields were still dying.

The flaw was not in the arithmetic.

It was in the person who thought arithmetic gave her the right to choose alone.

chapters.name: Many Witnesses
chapters.content:
By morning, the ruined seed bank had become a place people avoided looking at.

Its doors hung open beneath the corrugated roof. Inside, shelves held damp jars and split paper packets. Beans lay in blackening heaps. Orchard cuttings, wrapped in cloth, had softened at the stems. Farid walked past without acknowledging Nia.

Morrow was warm against her ribs, its single lens blinking red over the empty field.

“You’re filming an absence,” Jo said.

“I’m recording the condition.”

“You have a word for everything.”

Jo sat on an overturned water drum, lacing one boot. Since the convoy, she had spoken to Nia mostly in observations. You have a number. You have a reason. Each one landed with the soft force of a stone.

Across the yard, Sera had arranged three tables beneath a canvas awning. Copper wire, glass tubes, reagent strips, pressure gauges, weather meters, and handwritten forms covered the boards. The equipment looked crude beside Meridian’s sealed stations. It also looked possible.

“We begin with what can be checked,” Sera called. “Not what can be believed.”

Nia carried Morrow over.

Sera tapped its memory housing. “Your archive is valuable.”

“It’s the only continuous record of Node 7.”

“It’s a record copied by one fugitive from a system that edits records.”

“I didn’t edit it.”

“I know that. Do you know that?”

The question tightened around Nia.

Sera lifted a glass tube. A membrane divided the sample chamber from a strip of treated paper. “Independent stations. Simple enough for a farmer, a refugee child, or a municipal worker to operate. Every reading witnessed by more than one person. Every instrument numbered. Every disagreement preserved instead of corrected.”

Nia examined the tube. “Those won’t detect the unfamiliar solvent.”

“Not alone. But they will show conductivity, salts, acidity, pressure, and temperature. We can send samples to three laboratories and compare results. We can establish when wells change and whether the same event appears in different places.”

“We already have that.”

“We have your files.”

The words were not cruel. That made them worse.

By noon, the Open Current had divided the equipment. Stations would sit at Farid’s western well, the damaged canal, and the remaining seed field. Lio would carry two to the refugee camps beyond the freight road. Tomas had contacts among municipal workers who might install one in a southern district of Saint Orra. Other stations would be hidden in clinics, stairwells, and behind communal cisterns.

Nia studied the map.

“Three stations in the farms,” she said. “Two in the camps. One city station. That produces a rural bias.”

Farid, approaching from the irrigation gate, gave a short laugh. “The poisoned water is in the rural watershed.”

“And the people who drink it are everywhere.”

“Then put one in every place. Until you can, don’t call the first six a picture of the whole system.”

A boy with a red scarf tied around his arm stepped forward. Nia had seen him during the convoy, carrying filter membranes.

“The eastern camp has a clinic,” he said. “The western camp has no doctor and twice the children with rashes.”

“If you have confirmed contamination—”

“We have children,” he said.

“That isn’t a measurement.”

“It is why we need one.”

Nia looked at the map. Its symbols showed only locations. They did not show the clinic’s missing medicines, the distance between the western camp and clean water, or the hours mothers spent walking for it.

“Put the station in the western camp,” she said.

The boy blinked. “You’re sure?”

“No. I’m listening.”

That afternoon, Sera made everyone learn the instruments.

She poured clean water into one cup and a sample from Farid’s well into another. The difference was invisible. One test strip remained pale. The other stained faintly yellow.

“That could be handling,” Nia said.

“Good. What do you do?”

“Repeat the test.”

“With what?”

“A second strip from the same packet.”

“And if it disagrees?”

“Test a third.”

“And if all three disagree?”

“Record the disagreement.”

Sera smiled. “You may yet become tolerable.”

They taught field workers to calibrate pressure gauges against a sealed hand pump. Refugee children learned to number sample jars and tie witness tags around their necks. Lio explained that every reading would be copied onto paper before transmission. A signal could be jammed; a dozen notebooks hidden in different houses were harder to erase.

Morrow hovered above the awning, projecting a grid onto a sheet. Nia had written the station codes: F-01, F-02, C-01, R-01. Sera crossed out the legend.

“Who decided these codes?”

“I did.”

“Why do farms come before camps?”

“It makes sorting easier.”

“For whom?”

“Anyone using the archive.”

“Then let the people using it decide.”

The correction was small. It still felt like a hand reaching into the machinery of Nia’s mind.

They asked the children at the western camp what to call their station. After an argument, they chose Thirsty Crow, for the birds that gathered around the empty tanks and screamed at dawn. Farid’s workers named the canal station Mud Memory. The numbers remained underneath, but the names appeared first.

Near sunset, Nia crouched beside Hessa at the western well. Hessa had brought two jars from different depths.

“The shallow water tastes metallic after rain,” she said. “The deep water smells like hot stone.”

“When did you notice?”

“After the second storm. Before Meridian posted the contamination notice.”

“Did you report it?”

“To everyone who came to the well.”

Nia almost asked whether she had used an official channel. Instead she put away her stylus.

Hessa described the storm, the slick on the ditch, and the dead lizard near the culvert. She remembered which families stopped using the shallow pump and which could not afford to. She remembered a Helix truck parked by the northern fence three days before the water changed.

Her account was not a sensor reading. It was also not something the erased files could replace.

When Hessa finished, Nia asked permission to record her testimony. Hessa corrected Nia’s date by two days.

Nia changed it.

Farid waited at the edge of the field.

“You’re collecting stories now,” he said.

“I’m collecting witnesses.”

“Stories are not proof.”

“No. But proof without them can be made to mean anything.”

He glanced toward the seed bank. “If this project only makes a better accusation, I won’t help.”

“We need to prove Helix poisoned the watershed.”

“Then prove it. But if a station shows contamination, the people beside it need a plan. Water that can be cleaned. Soil that can hold a crop. Gates repaired before the next storm.”

“That could take resources away from the evidence.”

“Then the evidence is serving itself.”

Nia had no answer.

Farid stepped closer. “You asked the convoy model who would die first. Ask the watershed what it needs to live.”

After he left, Nia stayed beside the well until the light thinned over the fields.

Jo came carrying two cups of boiled tea and handed one to her.

“You were right,” Nia said.

“About which disaster?”

“The network. Meridian has an archive no one can inspect. Its conclusions are accepted because no one can reproduce them. I built the same thing with stolen files.”

“You built a locked room and put better evidence inside.”

Nia watched Morrow drift above the canal. “I thought control protected the data.”

“Control protected you from being challenged.”

“I was afraid someone would alter the readings.”

“Someone will.”

“I was afraid people would misunderstand them.”

“They will.”

“I was afraid the truth would be lost.”

Jo’s expression softened. “Then stop trying to be the place where it lives.”
